extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants evaluating claim subject-matter eligibility under the 2019 PEG
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (PEG) to evaluate whether patent claims satisfy Step 1, Step 2A (Prong One and Prong Two), and Step 2B for judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, mental processes, mathematical concepts, methods of organizing human activity) and whether additional claim elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory Category
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate Step 1: Does this claim fall within a statutory category?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition). Example: a claim reciting a series of steps is a 'process' and thus meets Step 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — Identify Abstract Idea & Map to PEG Groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that you believe recite an abstract idea, and determine whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas enumerated in the 2019 PEG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-part instruction: (a) point to the particular claimed limitations that embody the purported abstract idea; (b) decide whether that concept fits one or more PEG groupings (mathematical concepts; mental processes; certain methods of organizing human activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea grouping — Mathematical concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts include mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim's core is formulas/calculations/relationships, classify it here. Assess whether other claim elements meaningfully limit the mathematical concept (e.g., specific application of math to secure communications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea grouping — Mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental processes are concepts performed in the human mind (including an observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed concept can be performed in the human mind or is essentially mental, classify it here. Consider whether claimed physical/computational elements meaningfully tie the concept to a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea grouping — Certain methods of organizing human activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain methods of organizing human activity include fundamental economic principles or practices (including hedging, insurance, mitigating risk); commercial or legal interactions (agreements, contracts, advertising, marketing, sales, business relations); managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people (including social activities, teaching, and following rules or instructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed concept concerns management of relationships/interactions, commerce/legal activities, or personal behavior, it falls in this grouping. Example: a method that allows users to access and receive updates to medical records is treated as managing interactions between people and thus an abstract idea under this grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — Meaningful Limit / Integration into Practical Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there additional element(s) or a combination of elements in the claim that apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the additional elements (alone or in combination) integrate the exception into a practical application (i.e., meaningfully limit the abstract idea). Examples: cryptography claim — mathematical concepts used in a specific manner to secure communications (integration -> eligible); medical-records claim 1 — combination provides a specific improvement over prior art (integration -> eligible). By contrast, a claim that merely invokes generic computer components to implement the abstract idea at a high level (e.g., 'content server', 'generic network-based storage devices') and merely describes applying the idea on a computer does not impose meaningful limits and fails Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude WURC consideration in Step 2A Prong Two
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A Prong Two excludes evaluation of whether elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional (WURC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if additional elements are described in the background as conventional, that fact does not prevent those elements from integrating an abstract idea into a practical application under Prong Two. Do not dismiss integration solely because elements are WURC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Inventive Concept / 'Significantly More' Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claim provide an inventive concept, i.e., do the claim recite additional element(s) or a combination of elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception in the claim?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed additional elements transform the nature of the claim into patent-eligible subject matter by adding significantly more than the abstract idea. Mere recitation of generic computer components or routine data-handling steps at a high level is insufficient. The claim must recite specific improvements or unconventional features that provide 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation does not by itself make a claim eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: The performance of claim limitations using generic computer components (e.g., content server, generic network-based storage devices) does not preclude classification as an abstract idea, nor does it, by itself, integrate the idea into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that simply implement an abstract idea on a generic computer, without meaningful technological improvement or specific limitations, fail to satisfy Prong Two/Step 2B. Conversely, claims that show how the computer components are used in a specific, limiting, and practical way (e.g., solving a technical problem, securing communications via specific cryptographic use of math) can succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical-application evidence — specific improvements and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing that claimed elements use the judicial exception in a specific manner that sufficiently limits its use to a practical application supports eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for claim language and reasoning that ties abstract concepts to technical details or improvements (e.g., limiting use to transmitting ciphertext over a communication channel; relying on hardness of factoring to secure communications; providing real-time standardized updating across heterogeneous systems). Such concrete ties indicate integration into a practical application rather than mere drafting to monopolize an idea.
